original.math: Require compatible units, state spaces and maps. If the intended common structure is a gradient flow, specify ẋ=−K(x)∇E(x) with K positive semidefinite and show Ė≤0.
original.finish: Translate two concrete systems into the same formalism and prove the shared statement. A list of unrelated equations is not a derivation of unification.

entries.title: Bessel versus Parseval
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: The missing distinction in the original inequality list is completeness. Bessel’s inequality is an exact statement about projection error; Parseval’s equality appears when the chosen orthonormal family spans the relevant Hilbert space. A residual formula makes the practical meaning immediate.
definitions: Use an inner product linear in its first argument. For an orthonormal family e₁,…,e_m, define P_mx=Σ⟨x,e_j⟩e_j. Its span is a closed finite-dimensional subspace of the Hilbert space H.

result.name: Projection residual and completeness criterion
result.statement: For every x, ||x||²=Σ_{j=1}^m|⟨x,e_j⟩|²+||x−P_mx||². For a countable orthonormal family, the infinite coefficient sum is at most ||x||². Equality for every x holds exactly when its closed linear span is H.
result.proof: The residual is orthogonal to every e_j because taking its inner product with e_j subtracts the same coefficient. Pythagoras therefore splits the norm into projection and residual, and orthonormality gives the coefficient sum. Finite partial sums are increasing and bounded, so their limit exists. The partial projections form a Cauchy sequence, with squared differences equal to sums of omitted squared coefficients. Their limit projects onto the closed span. Equality means the residual projection onto the orthogonal complement vanishes. If equality holds for all x, that complement is zero and the span is dense.

example.setup: Take x=(2,3,6) in R³ and initially observe only e₁,e₂.
example.calculation: The observed squared coefficient sum is 4+9=13, total squared norm is 49, and residual squared norm is 36. Adding e₃ removes the residual exactly. Omitting e₃ never becomes harmless merely because the first two coefficients were calculated to high precision.
example.conclusion: This is both an approximation certificate and a statement of what the measurement family cannot see.

entries.limits: An infinite orthonormal family need not be complete. For nonorthogonal features, coefficients from raw inner products are not automatically orthogonal projections, and frame or Gram-matrix analysis is needed.
entries.extension: Develop a frame analogue with lower and upper frame bounds, or identify the cheapest observation family whose residual vanishes on a specified finite-dimensional model class.

original.concept: Bessel versus Parseval
original.origin: An inequality catalogue included Bessel, Hölder, Cauchy–Schwarz and Young.
original.question: What assumptions yield an inequality, and what extra completeness makes it an equality?
original.math: For an orthonormal family {e_k}, Σ|⟨x,e_k⟩|²≤||x||². Equality for every x requires completeness in the relevant Hilbert space.
original.finish: Compute a finite projection and its exact residual. Give a noncomplete-family example where the inequality is strict.

entries.title: Hölder and Young with equality cases
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: Conjugate exponents and equality cases turn a generic inequality into a sharp tool. The proof below also states what must be checked before applying it: measurability, the relevant integrability and the distinction between the absolute-value bound and the signed integral.
definitions: Let 1<p<∞ and q=p/(p−1), so 1/p+1/q=1. Norms are ||f||_p=(∫|f|^p)^(1/p) and the analogous q-norm, on one fixed measure space.

result.name: Young and Hölder with sharp equality
result.statement: For a,b≥0, ab≤a^p/p+b^q/q, with equality exactly when a^p=b^q. Consequently ∫|fg|≤||f||_p||g||_q. For nonzero finite norms, equality holds exactly when |f|^p/||f||_p^p=|g|^q/||g||_q^q almost everywhere.
result.proof: Fix a and minimize h(b)=b^q/q−ab+a^p/p over b≥0. Its derivative is b^(q−1)−a, with its unique minimum at b=a^(p−1), and the minimum equals zero. Normalize nonzero f,g to unit p- and q-norms, apply the scalar inequality pointwise and integrate. Equality in the integrated nonnegative difference requires pointwise equality almost everywhere, which yields the normalized-power condition. To obtain equality for |∫fg| as well, the product must also have an almost-everywhere constant phase or sign.

example.setup: Choose p=3, q=3/2, a=2 and b=4.
example.calculation: Here a^p=b^q=8, so Young is exact: ab=8=8/3+8/(3/2). For a finite counting measure, proportional normalized powers supply equally explicit Hölder equality examples. Choosing disjointly supported nonzero functions makes the product integral zero while both norms are positive, showing a strict case.
example.conclusion: The equality condition identifies when a proposed estimate is sharp and which directions are responsible for slack.

entries.limits: The endpoints p=1,q=∞ require essential-supremum language and a different equality statement. If either required norm is infinite, the finite useful estimate is unavailable even when a formal product expression can be written.
entries.extension: Use the equality characterization to optimize a linear functional on an L^p unit ball and compare existence and uniqueness in endpoint versus strictly convex cases.

original.finish: Derive Hölder from Young, state equality conditions and test a proposed application for the required integrability.

entries.title: Matrix norms and the quantity being bounded
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: Choosing a norm means choosing how input and output error are measured. A norm catalogue becomes useful only when attached to its induced error inequality. A two-dimensional example shows that several plausible norms report different numerical amplification.
definitions: The induced p-norm is ||A||_p=sup_{x≠0}||Ax||_p/||x||_p. The induced 1-norm is the largest absolute column sum, the induced infinity-norm is the largest absolute row sum, and the Frobenius norm is a Euclidean norm on entries.

result.name: Sharp induced bounds and singular-value comparisons
result.statement: For every vector x, ||Ax||_p≤||A||_p||x||_p. In Euclidean norm, ||A||₂ is the largest singular value, while ||A||_F² is the sum of squared singular values; hence ||A||₂≤||A||_F≤√r||A||₂ for rank r>0.
result.proof: The first inequality is the definition of the supremum. For p=1, triangle inequalities bound each output coordinate and collecting each |x_j| gives the maximum column sum; choosing a coordinate vector at a maximizing column attains it. The infinity case uses a maximizing row and matching signs. Orthogonal or unitary invariance reduces the Euclidean claims to a diagonal singular-value matrix, where the largest entry bounds their squared sum above and below. The rank-zero case has both norms zero.

example.calculation: Its induced 1- and infinity-norms are both three. Its Frobenius norm is √6. The eigenvalues of AᵀA=[[1,2],[2,5]] are 3±2√2, so ||A||₂=√(3+2√2)=1+√2. These are distinct measures of the same operator. A claim of amplification three is sharp for a 1-norm or infinity-norm question, but overestimates the sharp Euclidean factor.
example.conclusion: Reporting the input and output norms is part of stating the bound, not a cosmetic implementation detail.

entries.limits: Condition numbers also depend on the norm and require invertibility or a specified pseudoinverse/restricted subspace. An entrywise norm cannot replace an induced one without tracking the comparison constants.
entries.extension: For a chosen observation map, compute the restricted operator norm on the admissible state subspace and quantify how much a generic full-space bound overestimates the actual errors.

original.concept: Matrix norms and the quantity being bounded
original.origin: The operator 1-norm appeared alongside Frobenius and vector inequalities.
original.question: Which matrix norm corresponds to the input and output errors being measured?
original.math: The induced 1-norm is max_jΣ_i|aᵢⱼ|; the spectral norm is the largest singular value; the Frobenius norm is the square root of summed squared singular values.
original.finish: Compute all three on one nonnormal matrix, prove the desired error bound and avoid substituting a convenient norm without tracking constants.

entries.title: Lyapunov conditions in the right direction
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: A Lyapunov certificate is a sufficient argument tied to a chosen function. Failure of one function is not a system-instability certificate. The exact example below resolves that logical error and produces a contracting quadratic geometry for the same stable system.
definitions: For ẋ=Ax and symmetric P, define V(x)=xᵀPx. Positive definiteness P≻0 makes V comparable with ||x||². Along a trajectory, V̇=xᵀ(AᵀP+PA)x. A Hurwitz matrix has all eigenvalues in the open left half-plane.

result.name: Quadratic certificate and a counterexample to the failed converse
result.statement: If P≻0 and AᵀP+PA=−Q with Q≻0, then V(t)≤exp(−λ_min(Q)t/λ_max(P))V(0), proving exponential stability. A stable A can nevertheless make d||x||²/dt positive at some state.
result.proof: The derivative identity follows by the product rule. Since xᵀQx≥λ_min(Q)||x||² and V≤λ_max(P)||x||², V̇≤−[λ_min(Q)/λ_max(P)]V. Integration gives exponential decay of V; the lower eigenvalue bound on P translates this into a Euclidean state bound. The proof makes no assertion that every positive function has a negative derivative. For Hurwitz A, the integral P=∫₀∞exp(tAᵀ)Qexp(tA)dt provides the converse existence result, with convergence following from exponential matrix decay.

example.setup: Take A=[[-1,4],[0,−1]], whose eigenvalues are both −1.
example.calculation: At x=(1,1), Ax=(3,−1) and d(xᵀx)/dt=2xᵀAx=4>0. Yet P=[[1/2,1],[1,9/2]] has positive leading minor and determinant 5/4, and direct multiplication gives AᵀP+PA=−I. Thus the Euclidean norm can temporarily grow while the certified P-norm decreases.
example.conclusion: The apparent contradiction disappears once the certificate is interpreted in the right direction and its metric is stated.

entries.limits: A certificate for one linearization is not automatically a global nonlinear proof. Semidefinite Q needs an invariance argument for asymptotic convergence, and strict inequalities matter near marginal modes.
entries.extension: Find a common quadratic Lyapunov function for a specified family of matrices, or exhibit why switching among individually stable matrices defeats a proposed common bound.

entries.title: Units of the Einstein equation
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: Dimensional statements about tensor components must name the coordinate or frame convention. Using a local orthonormal frame and x⁰=ct makes the audit simple, while also explaining why coordinate components in other charts can carry different units.
definitions: Use metric signature (−,+,+,+), spacetime coordinates of length dimension, and a dimensionless orthonormal metric. Write G_N for Newton’s constant, c for speed, ε for energy density and G_μν for the Einstein tensor; the two symbols G have unrelated types.

result.name: A consistent dimensional audit of Einstein’s equation
result.statement: In this convention G_μν and Λg_μν have dimensions L⁻²; T_μν has dimensions ML⁻¹T⁻². Since [G_N]=L³M⁻¹T⁻² and [c⁴]=L⁴T⁻⁴, (G_N/c⁴)T_μν has dimension L⁻². The factor 8π is dimensionless and is not selected by dimensional analysis.
result.proof: A connection coefficient contains one derivative of a dimensionless metric, giving L⁻¹, and curvature has a derivative of the connection or a product of two connections, giving L⁻². Energy per volume is (ML²T⁻²)/L³=ML⁻¹T⁻². Multiplying exponents in G_N c⁻⁴T gives zero mass exponent, length exponent −2 and zero time exponent. The cosmological constant must have the same curvature dimension when it multiplies the dimensionless metric. All statements are frame and coordinate dependent at the component level, while the tensor equation is geometric.

example.setup: Consider a perfect-fluid stress tensor in its local rest frame.
example.calculation: T_00=ε and T_ii=p in the orthonormal convention, so pressure and energy density have matching units. If instead time is represented by t rather than ct, changing the coordinate basis introduces c factors into the time components; one must transform the tensor rather than recycle the orthonormal component units.
example.conclusion: The repaired equation is G_μν+Λg_μν=(8πG_N/c⁴)T_μν. It passes a dimensional audit without confusing Newton’s constant, curvature or matter units.

entries.limits: The audit cannot fix signs, the numerical coupling or a curvature convention. Those require definitions and a limiting calculation. Natural units c=1 suppress dimensions in notation but do not remove the need to restore them consistently.
entries.extension: Carry the same equation through an explicit coordinate rescaling and verify the transformed component units and physical observables.

entries.title: Why the coefficient is 8π
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: The coefficient 8π is determined by matching a conventioned relativistic field equation to Newtonian Poisson gravity. The trace reversal supplies a crucial factor one half. This is a derivation of the classical normalization, not a new gravitational law.
definitions: Set Λ=0 for the local weak-field limit. Use signature (−,+,+,+), x⁰=ct and R^ρ_{σμν}=∂_μΓ^ρ_{νσ}−∂_νΓ^ρ_{μσ}+Γ^ρ_{μα}Γ^α_{νσ}−Γ^ρ_{να}Γ^α_{μσ}, with R_σν=R^ρ_{σρν}. Let G_μν=κT_μν initially have an unknown κ.

result.name: Newtonian matching yields κ=8πG_N/c⁴
result.statement: For a static weak potential with g_00=−(1+2Φ/c²), slow matter and negligible pressure, R_00≈∇²Φ/c² and the trace-reversed source is T_00−g_00T/2≈ρc²/2. Matching ∇²Φ=4πG_Nρ therefore gives κ=8πG_N/c⁴.
result.proof: Contract the field equation in four dimensions: −R=κT. Substituting back gives R_μν=κ(T_μν−g_μνT/2). For dust at rest, T_00≈ρc², spatial diagonal stresses are negligible, and T≈−ρc²; with g_00≈−1 the displayed source becomes ρc²−ρc²/2. The weak, static connection is Γ^i_{00}≈∂_iΦ/c². In R_00, time derivatives vanish and connection products are higher order, leaving ∂_iΓ^i_{00}≈∇²Φ/c². Thus ∇²Φ=(κc⁴/2)ρ. Equating its coefficient with Poisson’s coefficient fixes κ.

example.setup: Track the factors before inserting the answer.
example.calculation: If one incorrectly equates R_00 with κρc² without trace reversal, the inferred coupling would differ by a factor of two. If one uses time rather than ct, the connection and stress components must both be rescaled. Either mistake can produce superficially plausible but inconsistent equations.
example.conclusion: The numerical factor and powers of c are fixed together once geometric, matter and Newtonian conventions are stated.

entries.limits: This leading-order derivation assumes weak fields, slow motion, small stresses and a regime in which Λ is negligible. Reversing the Riemann-tensor sign requires changing the field-equation sign convention consistently. The result does not derive Einstein’s equation uniquely from Newtonian gravity.
entries.extension: Continue to the first post-Newtonian corrections and identify which additional observations distinguish relativistic field equations sharing the same Newtonian limit.

entries.title: Sixteen entries but ten independent components
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: There are several counts in general relativity, and conflating them produces incorrect conclusions. Matrix entries, independent tensor components, differential identities, initial-data constraints and physical propagating modes belong to different stages of the analysis.
definitions: Use indices μ,ν∈{0,1,2,3}. A symmetric covariant tensor satisfies S_μν=S_νμ. The Einstein tensor obeys four contracted Bianchi identities. In a 3+1 formulation, the spatial metric and its conjugate momentum have six components each.

result.name: Component count and local vacuum degree-of-freedom count
result.statement: A symmetric four-by-four tensor has ten independent components: four diagonal and six off-diagonal. The four contracted Bianchi identities are differential identities, not four duplicate entries. For regular vacuum general relativity, four first-class constraints acting on twelve spatial canonical variables leave four physical phase-space variables, or two configuration polarizations per spatial point.
result.proof: For an n-by-n symmetric matrix there are n diagonal entries and n(n−1)/2 unordered off-diagonal pairs, giving n(n+1)/2. At n=4 this is ten, although the full display contains sixteen slots. The Bianchi relations differentiate combinations of field-equation components; they do not identify any selected four slots algebraically. In the canonical count, a first-class constraint imposes one phase-space condition and generates one gauge direction. Four such constraints therefore remove eight of the twelve spatial canonical variables. Dividing the remaining four phase-space variables into coordinate-momentum pairs gives two local propagating degrees of freedom.

example.setup: Write the first row as S_00,S_01,S_02,S_03 and the remaining rows with S_10=S_01 and the corresponding symmetries.
example.calculation: There is no S_44 in the chosen zero-through-three convention. A one-through-four convention may use it, but mixing the two is invalid. In a linearized plane-wave gauge, the remaining transverse-traceless amplitudes can be represented by h_+ and h_×, illustrating rather than replacing the constrained Hamiltonian count.
example.conclusion: The repaired statement retains all ten independent equations while explaining their differential dependence and gauge structure.

entries.limits: Boundary conditions, global moduli, matter fields and singular constraint surfaces can affect global degrees of freedom. Subtracting four identities from ten components is not on its own a derivation of two propagating modes.
entries.extension: Perform an explicit linearized gauge reduction for a plane wave and compare it with the canonical count in a stated background and boundary setting.

entries.title: Covariant conservation is a structural condition
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: Covariant conservation is the compatibility condition supplied by the geometry of the field equation. It does not say that coordinate components are constant, or that a global conserved total energy exists in every spacetime. A homogeneous expanding metric gives an exact example of the distinction.
definitions: For the Levi-Civita connection, ∇g=0 and the contracted Bianchi identity is ∇^μG_μν=0. Let κ and Λ be constants. A perfect fluid has rest energy density ε, pressure p and four-velocity normalized by u·u=−1 in a c=1 convention.

result.name: Source conservation and the FLRW continuity equation
result.statement: The field equation G_μν+Λg_μν=κT_μν with κ≠0 implies ∇^μT_μν=0. In a homogeneous FLRW metric, this includes ε̇+3H(ε+p)=0, where H=ȧ/a. For constant equation-of-state parameter p=wε, εa^{3(1+w)} is constant.
result.proof: Apply the covariant divergence to the field equation. The geometric identity and metric compatibility eliminate the left side, and constant κ gives the conclusion. In comoving FLRW coordinates, expanding ∇_μT^{μ0}=0 combines the ordinary time derivative of ε with the connection terms associated with the changing spatial volume a³; isotropic pressure contributes three identical work terms. Substitution p=wε yields d logε/dt=−3(1+w)d loga/dt, whose integral gives the power law wherever ε and a are positive.

example.setup: Compare dust and radiation under a scale factor that doubles.
example.calculation: For dust w=0, energy density falls by 2³=8. For radiation w=1/3, it falls by 2⁴=16. Neither changing component violates covariant conservation. The additional radiation factor expresses the pressure-work or redshift contribution in this model.
example.conclusion: A conservation law can involve geometric transport and changing volume. Ordinary component constancy is not the right test.

entries.limits: A global conserved charge generally needs an appropriate symmetry or boundary construction. If κ or Λ varies, additional derivative terms enter and the simple inference must be revised. Matter models must satisfy their own evolution equations consistently.
entries.extension: Given a Killing field ξ, derive conservation of J^μ=T^{μν}ξ_ν for symmetric covariantly conserved T, and identify the boundary conditions needed to turn it into a constant integrated charge.

original.math: ∇^μG_μν=0 and metric compatibility imply ∇^μT_μν=0 for constant coupling and Λ. This is covariant conservation, not a claim that all coordinate components are spatially constant.
original.finish: Demonstrate the identity in a stated geometry and distinguish local stress-energy conservation from a globally defined total energy.

entries.title: Grothendieck universes and their logical cost
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: Universe language is a relative-size discipline backed by a set-theoretic assumption. It is not a mechanism for eliminating every paradox without cost. The useful mathematical task is to state the closure axioms and show exactly which categorical constructions they permit.
definitions: A Grothendieck universe U is a transitive set closed under pairing, power sets and unions indexed by a set belonging to U, with the family’s members in U. To support ordinary infinite mathematics one asks ω∈U. A U-small set is an element of U, which differs from merely being a subset of U.

result.name: The inaccessible-cardinal construction of a universe
result.statement: If κ is a strongly inaccessible cardinal, then V_κ is a Grothendieck universe containing ω. Consequently U-small sets, maps, finite products and function sets can be handled inside one fixed relative-size level. The existence of such an uncountable inaccessible cardinal is an additional assumption, not a theorem of bare ZFC.
result.proof: Transitivity of the cumulative hierarchy is immediate. If x,y∈V_κ, their ranks are below κ, so pairing and power sets still have rank below κ because κ is a limit ordinal. For an indexed family (x_i)_{i∈I} with I∈V_κ, strong inaccessibility ensures every set in V_κ has cardinality below κ. Regularity then bounds the supremum of the fewer-than-κ ranks of x_i below κ, so their union remains in V_κ. For function sets X→Y, their graphs are subsets of X×Y and are therefore contained in a suitable iterated power-set construction inside U.

example.setup: Take two U-small sets X and Y.
example.calculation: Ordered pairs can be constructed by the Kuratowski definition, yielding X×Y∈U. Every function graph lies in P(X×Y), and the collection of all such graphs is a subset of that power set, hence U-small under the closure axioms. By contrast, the entire collection of all U-small sets is U itself; asserting U∈U would contradict foundation. It belongs to a larger universe only when another size assumption is made.
example.conclusion: The construction makes size bookkeeping precise while retaining a visible logical boundary.

entries.limits: This treatment proves the conditional construction, not consistency or existence of inaccessible cardinals. Degenerate finite universes and conventions excluding or including ω must be distinguished. Different foundational treatments can avoid universe axioms for specific constructions.
entries.extension: Rebuild one category-of-structures construction using a fixed cardinal bound instead, then compare its smallness guarantees with the universe-based version.

entries.title: Stirling partitions do not supply torsional energy
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: The original torsion comparison combined two unrelated notions of structure: set partitions and elastic deformation. Both can be developed, but a counting theorem does not determine an energy. An explicit discrete energy and continuum limit provide the missing bridge when an actual rod model is intended.
definitions: S(N,k) counts partitions of N labeled objects into k nonempty unlabeled subsets. A contiguous partition of an ordered chain instead cuts k−1 of its N−1 gaps. For a rod of length L, θ(x) is an angular displacement and GJ>0 is a torsional stiffness parameter.

result.name: Distinct partition counts and a consistent torsional energy
result.statement: Arbitrary partitions satisfy S(N,k)=kS(N−1,k)+S(N−1,k−1); contiguous k-block partitions number C(N−1,k−1). For grid spacing h=L/N, E_N=(GJ/2)Σ_{i=0}^{N−1}[(θ_{i+1}−θ_i)/h]²h equals the continuum Dirichlet energy of the piecewise-linear interpolant.
result.proof: For Stirling’s recurrence, the last label either joins one of k existing blocks or forms a singleton. For contiguous partitions, choosing the cut gaps is a bijection. For energy, the interpolant derivative is constant on each grid interval and equals the difference quotient; integrating its squared derivative gives the formula exactly. Thus strong H¹ convergence of interpolants implies energy convergence. A bounded-energy sequence with a fixed endpoint has an H¹ bound; weak lower semicontinuity gives a lower energy bound at weak limits, while interpolating smooth functions supplies elementary recovery approximations. No set-partition count is needed for this argument.

example.setup: First take N=4,k=2, then a constant total twist Θ.
example.calculation: The partition counts are seven and three respectively. For θ_i=Θi/N, every difference quotient is Θ/L and E_N=GJΘ²/(2L) for every N. For L=GJ=1 and θ(x)=x², endpoint interpolation gives E_N=2/3−1/(6N²), converging to (1/2)∫₀¹4x²dx=2/3.
example.conclusion: The continuum energy follows from a stated stiffness law and interpolation, not from taking a limit of the Stirling numbers.

entries.limits: The one-dimensional quadratic energy assumes a chosen linear elastic model. Material nonlinearities, warping, varying stiffness and topology of configurations require additional specification. Algebraic torsion in a group is a different concept again.
entries.extension: If partitions represent actual latent material domains, define a weighted sum over contiguous partitions with a stated domain energy and examine its continuum or large-system limit.

entries.title: Vector motion and rotation conventions
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: Movement commands can be formulated without ambiguous appeals to trigonometry. Linear algebra combines the local commands; a rotation converts the resulting vector into another frame. Keeping magnitude conventions explicit resolves diagonal-speed discrepancies.
definitions: In a right-handed plane use column vectors and counterclockwise rotation R(θ)=[[cosθ,−sinθ],[sinθ,cosθ]]. Let a local command u=(u₁,u₂) specify components in orthonormal local axes. World velocity is v=su rotated by R, namely v=sR(θ)u.

result.name: Rotation preserves speed but raw diagonal input changes it
result.statement: Because RᵀR=I, ||v||₂=s||u||₂. A single unit-axis command has speed s, while raw input u=(1,1) has speed s√2. Normalizing nonzero input by its Euclidean norm produces constant speed s regardless of its direction.
result.proof: Multiply the displayed matrix by its transpose and use cos²θ+sin²θ=1 and cancellation of the cross terms. Taking squared norms then gives the identity. The difference between axis and diagonal commands follows from ||(1,0)||=1 and ||(1,1)||=√2. If the desired control preserves analog intensity below unit radius, the mapping u↦u/max(1,||u||) leaves small commands unchanged and caps only those outside the unit disk. This is a specified control law, not a consequence forced by coordinate geometry.

example.setup: Use the exact rotation with cosθ=3/5 and sinθ=4/5.
example.calculation: The unit forward command maps to (3/5,4/5), of squared norm one. The unnormalized diagonal maps to (−1/5,7/5), of squared norm two. Its normalized version divides both components by √2, returning squared norm one. These checks use exact rational arithmetic before the final normalization.
example.conclusion: Coordinate conversion and speed policy can be independently tested. This makes it possible to change a frame without silently changing the physical or numerical interpretation of commands.

entries.limits: Nonorthogonal coordinate bases, perspective projection, acceleration limits and a non-Euclidean metric alter the formula or the appropriate norm. Time-dependent frames introduce additional derivative terms when differentiating positions.
entries.extension: Specify an anisotropic metric or acceleration constraint, then derive the admissible velocity set and a frame-consistent control projection onto it.

entries.title: A proposed analogy needs a dimensionless correspondence
entries.status: Classical result developed and worked
entries.summary: A spectral analogy becomes mathematical only when state spaces, operators, units and observables are related by an explicit map. A small periodic hopping model supplies a genuine Bloch calculation, while a similarity-transform example separates shared eigenvalues from shared dynamics.
definitions: Consider a two-site unit cell on an infinite one-dimensional lattice with real hoppings t₁,t₂. Its Hermitian Bloch matrix is H(k)=[[0,t₁+t₂e^(−ik)],[t₁+t₂e^(ik),0]], where k is a dimensionless crystal phase. Hopping parameters and eigenvalues have a common energy unit.

result.name: An explicit band gap and a warning about spectral equivalence
result.statement: The two bands are E_±(k)=±√(t₁²+t₂²+2t₁t₂cosk). Their minimum separation is 2||t₁|−|t₂||. Equality of eigenvalue sets in another model does not establish equivalence of observation maps or Euclidean amplification.
result.proof: The characteristic polynomial is E²−|t₁+t₂e^(−ik)|². Expanding the squared modulus gives the dispersion relation. Its minimum is (|t₁|−|t₂|)² because cosk ranges over [−1,1]. If B=SAS⁻¹, A and B share characteristic polynomials, but exp(tB)=S exp(tA)S⁻¹ and Euclidean norm bounds acquire the condition number of S. Only a unitary S preserves every Euclidean norm and the inner-product structure automatically. Observables must also transform, for example C_B=C_A S⁻¹, to preserve measured outputs.

example.setup: Take t₁=2,t₂=1 and compare an unrelated rescaled two-state model.
example.calculation: The bands at k=0 are ±3 and at k=π are ±1, so the gap is two. To transfer this statement, another model must supply a compatible periodic operator, an energy-scale conversion and a map respecting the relevant measurements. A match between an energy number and some unrelated flux number has no meaning until units and maps are supplied.
example.conclusion: This example yields an actual operator theorem and a precise test for proposed cross-domain correspondences.

entries.limits: The toy model does not establish that another physical system has Bloch periodicity, the same Hilbert space or the same operator domain. Isospectral operators can remain distinguishable by eigenvectors, locality and response functions.
entries.extension: Classify intertwiners BS=SA that also preserve a chosen observation map, and determine which spectral or transport identities survive after taking dimensionless variables.

entries.title: Residual energy and exact Gaussian calibration
entries.status: Developed classical result with worked example
entries.summary: The original squared-deviation formula becomes useful once its units, reference model and covariance are specified. A squared residual is a geometric discrepancy. An entropy is a functional of a probability distribution. Neither name determines the other.
definitions: Let r=X−μ∈Rᵈ. The raw residual energy is E=rᵀr. If Σ is a specified positive-definite covariance, the whitened discrepancy is Q=rᵀΣ⁻¹r.
Here μ and Σ are known constants under the null model, rather than estimates obtained from the same observations.

result.name: Whitened Gaussian discrepancy
result.statement: If X has multivariate normal distribution N(μ,Σ) with Σ positive definite, then Q has the χ² distribution with d degrees of freedom. Consequently E[Q]=d and Var(Q)=2d. The unweighted E generally depends on the coordinate units.
result.proof: Factor Σ=LLᵀ with L invertible and put Z=L⁻¹r. The change-of-variables formula gives independent standard normal coordinates Z₁,…,Z_d. Then Q=ZᵀZ=ΣZᵢ². Its moment-generating function is the product (1−2t)^(−d/2), obtained by completing the square in each one-dimensional Gaussian integral. Differentiation at zero gives the stated moments. Changing the scale of one coordinate changes E but is canceled by the corresponding covariance transformation in Q.

example.setup: Take r=(1,2) and Σ=diag(1,4).
example.calculation: The raw residual is E=1+4=5. Whitening gives Z=(1,1), so Q=2. If both coordinates are expressed in ten times larger numerical units, r becomes (10,20) and Σ becomes diag(100,400); E becomes 500, whereas Q remains 2.
example.conclusion: The standardized discrepancy is dimensionless and has an exact reference distribution under the declared Gaussian null. It has not thereby become Shannon entropy.

entries.limits: Estimating means, regression coefficients or covariance from the same sample changes the null distribution. In ordinary known-variance linear regression, orthogonal projection gives n−p residual degrees of freedom; estimated covariance can instead lead to F or other statistics. Nonnormal residuals need separate calibration.
entries.extension: Study how Q changes under covariance uncertainty by bounding it between eigenvalue-controlled quadratic forms. This produces an honest robustness interval rather than assigning an entropy interpretation to a residual.

original.concept: Rename and calibrate Entropy Squared
original.origin: The old ES=Σ(X_k−E_k)² expression was called Entropy Squared.
original.question: Is the intended quantity a residual energy, a standardized discrepancy or an information divergence?
original.math: Σ(X_k−E_k)² is a squared Euclidean residual and has squared measurement units. With known positive-definite covariance Σ, rᵀΣ⁻¹r is dimensionless; Shannon entropy and KL divergence are different objects.
original.finish: Compute all three on a common example, specify the probability model and derive a calibration rather than assigning an entropy interpretation by name.

entries.title: The chain rule as a statement about local linear maps
entries.status: Developed classical result with worked example
entries.summary: The derivative is the linear part of a local approximation. The chain rule composes these linear parts and tracks their domains; a secant slope or a scalar symbol does not replace a multivariable derivative.
definitions: For differentiable g:Rᵐ→Rⁿ and f:Rⁿ→Rᵏ, Dg(x):Rᵐ→Rⁿ and Df(g(x)):Rⁿ→Rᵏ are linear maps.
Differentiability means g(x+h)=g(x)+Dg(x)h+o(||h||), with the remainder small relative to ||h||.

result.name: Typed chain rule
result.statement: D(f∘g)(x)=Df(g(x))Dg(x). If a scalar F has Hessian operator norm at most M along the segment from x to x+h, its linearization remainder is at most M||h||²/2.
result.proof: Insert the differentiability expansion of g into the expansion of f at g(x). Since g(x+h)−g(x)=O(||h||), the outer remainder is o(||h||). The coefficient of h is exactly the displayed composition. For the second statement, integrate the directional derivative along the segment twice; the second integral is ∫₀¹(1−t)hᵀH_F(x+th)h dt, whose absolute value is bounded by M||h||²/2.

example.setup: Let g(u,v)=(u²+v,eᵘ) and f(a,b)=ab, so F(u,v)=(u²+v)eᵘ.
example.calculation: Dg=[[2u,1],[eᵘ,0]], while Df(g)=[eᵘ,u²+v]. Multiplication gives DF=[eᵘ(2u+u²+v),eᵘ]. At (1,2), DF=(5e,e). Direct differentiation of F gives the same row vector and therefore independently checks the composition order.
example.conclusion: A perturbation (h₁,h₂) changes F to first order by 5eh₁+eh₂. The two inputs have different sensitivities; one scalar slope would omit that distinction.

entries.limits: The Hessian remainder bound requires a neighborhood with a uniform bound. A pointwise derivative alone supplies no global finite-step error estimate. Nondifferentiable coordinate changes need different calculus.
entries.extension: For a long computation, propagate both Jacobians and explicit remainder bounds. This distinguishes a mathematically controlled sensitivity estimate from an uncalibrated finite-difference plot.

original.concept: Slope, differentiation and the chain rule
