syntheses.title: An exact robust Gaussian sensor panel with a strict greedy gap and a blind direction
syntheses.status: Constructed finite model proved and exhaustively certified
syntheses.summary: This worked design turns the projection formula in S006 into a complete exact optimization problem. Six coordinate channels, six declared mean-shift centers, nonuniform costs and six uncertainty balls give a unique cost13 optimum. A fully specified gain-per-cost greedy rule instead costs16. Every channel participates in an inclusion-minimal feasible panel, no single channel is cost-dominated, and none of the six fault constraints is implied by the others. A deliberately withheld direction is nevertheless invisible to the optimum panel. All of these claims concern this constructed mathematical instance, with no empirical dataset or application-performance claim.
definitions: Let X∼N(μ+d+e,I₆), with a known baseline μ and deterministic mean shift d+e. A coordinate panel S⊆{A,B,C,D,E,F} observes the selected coordinates. Its centered squared statistic T_S=Σ_{i∈S}(X_i−μ_i)² has a noncentral χ²_|S| law with noncentrality λ_S(d+e)=Σ_{i∈S}(d_i+e_i)². The empty panel is allowed in the finite enumeration but cannot meet the positive target.

The six costs and coverage sets are A:(6,{1,3,5}), B:(7,{1,2,3}), C:(6,{4}), D:(6,{2,3,5,6}), E:(7,{2,4,5,6}), F:(4,{1,6}). Define the six rational centers by d⁽ʲ⁾_i=2 when channel i covers target j and zero otherwise. Thus d⁽¹⁾=(2,2,0,0,0,2), d⁽²⁾=(0,2,0,2,2,0), d⁽³⁾=(2,2,0,2,0,0), d⁽⁴⁾=(0,0,2,0,2,0), d⁽⁵⁾=(2,0,0,2,2,0), and d⁽⁶⁾=(0,0,0,2,2,2).

For each center, the declared uncertainty set is the full Euclidean ball ||e||₂≤1 in six-dimensional whitened coordinates. Feasibility means inf_{||e||≤1}λ_S(d⁽ʲ⁾+e)≥1 for every j=1,…,6. Costs add across selected channels. Noncentrality is the declared design criterion; panels of different sizes have different null degrees of freedom and require their own significance calibration.

The greedy heuristic starts with no channels. At each step it chooses the unused channel maximizing the number of newly satisfied target constraints divided by its cost; ties would be settled alphabetically. It stops when all six constraints are satisfied. There are no maximizing ties along the path in this instance.

result.name: Exact robust-margin reduction and a unique finite optimum
result.statement: For any orthogonal coordinate projection P_S and ε≥0, inf_{||e||≤ε}||P_S(d+e)||²=max(||P_Sd||−ε,0)². Consequently the declared ε=1,target1 problem is feasible exactly when every center has selected energy at least4. The unique minimum-cost panel is {A,E}, of cost13. Greedy selects D,F,C and has cost16, a strict ratio16/13. The optimum is blind to the withheld center d*=2e_D, whose full-observation noncentrality is4.
result.proof:
Triangle inequality and ||P_Se||≤||e|| give ||P_S(d+e)||≥max(||P_Sd||−ε,0). If ||P_Sd||>ε, choose e=−εP_Sd/||P_Sd||. If ||P_Sd||≤ε, choose e=−P_Sd. Both perturbations are allowed and attain the bound, including the zero case. For positive target1 and ε=1, the inequality max(√λ−1,0)²≥1 is equivalent to λ≥4. Every nonzero center coordinate is2, so the energy condition is equivalent to selecting at least one channel from that target’s coverage support. The statistical robustness problem has therefore reduced exactly, without approximation, to this declared weighted set-cover instance.

The panel A,E covers all targets and costs13. Any feasible panel containing C needs at least two additional channels: no pair C plus one other channel covers all six targets. The cheapest possible two other channels cost4+6, so such a panel costs at least16. A feasible panel not containing C must contain E, because only C and E cover target4. At total cost at most13, E can be accompanied by at most one other channel, since the two cheapest remaining costs are4 and6. E alone fails; E,F misses target3; E,D misses target1; E,A succeeds and costs13; E,B exceeds the budget. Thus A,E is the unique feasible panel at cost at most13. This gives an analytic optimality and uniqueness certificate in addition to the enumeration.

Initially D has gain/cost4/6=2/3, uniquely larger than E’s4/7 or any other ratio. After D, the missing targets are1 and4. F supplies target1 at ratio1/4, uniquely beating A’s1/6 and the other choices. After D,F only target4 remains; C’s1/6 beats E’s1/7. Greedy therefore returns D,F,C of total cost16. No claim is made that this heuristic is worst possible, or that the example estimates its usual behavior.

For the withheld vector2e_D, P_{A,E}d*=0. Its selected Gaussian law is exactly the same as the baseline law. Hence every test using only those observed coordinates, including repeated independent samples, has the same rejection probability under this alternative as under the null. Full observation retains norm2 and worst-case noncentrality(2−1)²=1 under the same unit uncertainty. More generally, any rank-k linear panel with k<6 has a nonzero kernel. Selecting an appropriately scaled shift in that kernel proves that no such panel can preserve all mean-shift directions. This is an information obstruction, not a failure of the finite optimization certificate.

example.setup: The portable supplement_verify.py enumerates every one of the2⁶=64 coordinate panels. It records the selected channels, integer cost, six integer center energies, covered-target list and feasibility flag. It also records the exact greedy candidates at every step, inclusion-minimal panels and witnesses that each target constraint is necessary.
example.calculation:
There are34 feasible panels. The optimum A,E has center energies(4,4,4,4,8,4). Its six exact worst-case noncentralities are(1,1,1,1,9−4√2,1). For the five energy4 centers, subtracting one unit in their sole active retained coordinate attains1. For target5, subtract(1/√2,1/√2) in coordinates A,E; this perturbation has norm1 and attains9−4√2. Greedy D,F,C has center energies(4,4,4,4,4,8), and its minimum robust margin is also1 for the declared targets, at the higher cost16. A withheld center2e_D has selected noncentrality0 in A,E but4 in D,F,C and the full panel. For the simple Gaussian center alternative, the selected Kullback–Leibler divergence from baseline is half the selected noncentrality, so it is zero for the withheld direction in the optimum panel.

To see that the six channels and six constraints are substantive, inspect the additional exact witnesses. No channel has its entire target set contained in that of another channel of equal or smaller cost. Each channel belongs to at least one inclusion-minimal feasible panel. For each target j, selecting all channels that do not cover j satisfies the other five targets and fails exactly j. Thus no target constraint is implied by the other five. The verifier checks all these finite properties rather than relying on a picture of the incidence matrix.
example.conclusion: The finite optimum is exact, has a strict cost advantage over the stated greedy rule, and remains unable to guarantee unlisted directions. The constructive counterexample is compatible with all the declared-target certificates. Exact optimization, robustness to a specified ball, detector calibration and universal observability are distinct questions that can now be stated and checked separately.

syntheses.limits: This is a deliberately constructed six-channel Gaussian location model with known identity covariance and additive deterministic mean uncertainty. Its costs, centers and radius are mathematical inputs, not measured quantities. The objective constrains worst-case noncentrality; it is not an empirical accuracy guarantee, and equal noncentralities in different degrees of freedom do not by themselves imply equal test power. Estimated covariance, covariance-changing faults, temporal dependence, nonlinear sensors and unmodeled shifts need separate analysis. The withheld vector demonstrates a scope boundary and does not invalidate optimality for the declared family. The general robust-margin formula is classical projection geometry, and the small exact instance is an illustrative certificate rather than a claim of new general optimization theory.
syntheses.extension: Replace identity covariance by a fixed rational positive-definite matrix Σ and let each nonempty panel measure specified linear combinations with a full-row-rank matrix B. Then BΣBᵀ is invertible and λ_S=dᵀK_Bd, where K_B=Bᵀ(BΣBᵀ)⁻¹B; state the uncertainty ball in whitened coordinates. When B and Σ are rational, K_B is rational. The Euclidean orthogonal projector in whitened coordinates is instead P=Σ^(1/2)K_BΣ^(1/2), which need not be rational: for Σ=diag(1,2) and B=(1,1), K_B is the all-ones matrix divided by3, whereas P=[[1,√2],[√2,2]]/3. Redundant measurement rows require a separately stated pseudoinverse and observation-rank convention. For finitely many candidate full-row-rank panels, exhaustive enumeration still certifies the optimum, although robust thresholds can involve algebraic numbers. A further exact task is to classify the parameter cells in costs or radii where the optimal panel changes, while retaining the nullspace impossibility for any universal dimension reduction.

syntheses.title: Exact tree synchronization certificates and observable phase information
syntheses.status: Full nondegenerate tree branch classification and quantitative bounds proved here; rational examples verified; no general cyclic or global-convergence claim
syntheses.summary: A finite tree makes the nonlinear locking problem unusually exact: every edge flow is fixed by a cut sum, the cohesive phase differences follow by arcsine, and stability is certified by a positive weighted Laplacian. The same calculation separates dynamic stability from observability. Relative-phase measurements lose common phase and common frequency, while even a stable synchronized star has exact nonlinear motions invisible to a center-only sensor. The locking criterion is classical; the derivation, rational certificate, sensitivity bounds and observation examples here are an explicit synthesis, not a claim of a newly discovered synchronization theorem.
definitions: Let T=(V,E) be an undirected connected tree with n≥2 vertices, arbitrarily oriented edges and incidence matrix B∈R^(n×(n−1)). A column has −1 at its tail and +1 at its head. Every edge has coupling K_e>0.
Use the symmetric Kuramoto equation θ̇=ω−B diag(K)sin(Bᵀθ), componentwise sine. Since 1ᵀB=0, mean frequency is Ω=(1/n)1ᵀω. In the rotating frame set b=ω−Ω1, so 1ᵀb=0 and θ̇=b−B diag(K)sin(Bᵀθ).

General phase states lie on (R/2πZ)^n modulo the diagonal common-phase circle. A cohesive lift has δ=Bᵀθ with |δ_e|<π/2. Fixing 1ᵀθ=0 removes the common-phase direction locally. For 0<γ<π/2 one can instead impose the closed bound |δ_e|≤γ.
For each oriented edge e, remove it and let H_e be the component containing its head. Define the cut flow f_e=Σ_(i∈H_e)b_i. At a locked state the flow equation is Bf=b.
The linearization at a cohesive locked state is η̇=−L_wη, where L_w=B diag(w)Bᵀ and w_e=K_e cosδ_e=√(K_e²−f_e²)>0. Let λ₂ denote the least positive Laplacian eigenvalue.

result.name: Necessary and sufficient tree locking, local stability, boundary sensitivity and observability
result.statement: If every |f_e|<K_e, there are exactly 2^(n−1) locked equilibria on the phase torus modulo common phase. Each edge independently selects arcsin(f_e/K_e) or π−arcsin(f_e/K_e), modulo 2π. An equilibrium with q negative edge cosines has exactly q unstable linear directions on the phase quotient; there are C(n−1,q) such equilibria. Thus precisely one branch, with all edge cosines positive, is locally exponentially stable and cohesive. A state with |δ_e|≤γ<π/2 exists exactly when |f_e|≤K_e sinγ for every edge. If any |f_e|>K_e there is no locked equilibrium; if exactly r edges saturate and the others are strictly feasible, the count becomes 2^(n−1−r) and the quotient Hessian has r zero directions. For the stable branch, edge-flow sensitivity is ∂δ_e/∂f_e=1/w_e. The rate bounds are min_e(w_e)λ₂(BBᵀ)≤λ₂(L_w)≤n w_e/[s(n−s)] for every edge separating s and n−s vertices. A full relative-phase panel leaves only common phase unobservable and a uniform natural-frequency shift unidentifiable; a restricted center-only star sensor can miss additional exact nonlinear trajectories.
result.proof:
First prove the cut formula. A connected tree has n−1 edges and B has full column rank. One elementary proof removes a leaf: a zero-divergence flow has zero flow on its only incident edge, and induction removes all edges. The column image is contained in 1⊥ and has dimension n−1, so it equals 1⊥. Thus Bf=b has exactly one solution. Summing the divergence equation over H_e cancels every internal edge and leaves +f_e at the unique crossing edge, giving the displayed cut sum. Conversely those sums produce the unique solution; this can also be constructed by repeatedly eliminating leaves. No nonlinear approximation has been made.

At an equilibrium, f_e=K_e sinδ_e. Strict cohesion forces |f_e|<K_e and gives the unique principal value δ_e=arcsin(f_e/K_e). On a tree, any collection of real edge differences lifts to node phases: choose a root phase and integrate differences along the unique root-to-node path. There are no cycle-sum compatibility conditions. Subtracting the node mean fixes the chosen gauge. This proves sufficiency and uniqueness modulo common phase. Replacing the interval by [−γ,γ] gives precisely |f_e|≤K_e sinγ because sine is strictly increasing there. For a graph with cycles, the integration step can fail even when individual edge bounds hold, so this proof must not be extended merely by reusing its inequalities.

For the full branch classification, consider phase differences modulo 2π rather than restricting to the principal interval. Each strict scalar equation sinδ_e=f_e/K_e has exactly two distinct circle solutions, with cosines of opposite sign. A tree integrates every edge assignment uniquely modulo common phase, so there are exactly 2^(n−1) equilibria. On 1⊥ the linear map T=Bᵀ is an isomorphism. The quotient Hessian quadratic form is x↦(Tx)ᵀdiag(K_e cosδ_e)(Tx), and Sylvester’s law of inertia therefore gives exactly one negative direction per negative edge cosine, one positive direction per positive cosine and one zero direction per saturated edge. The dynamics has the negative of this Hessian as its Jacobian, so q negative cosines give q unstable eigenvalues. Choosing the q negative branches among n−1 edges gives C(n−1,q). All-positive cosines give the unique local minimum; every other nondegenerate branch is a saddle or the all-negative repeller. If r edges saturate, each of those sine equations has only one circle solution, giving 2^(n−1−r) equilibria with r extra linear zero directions. These boundary statements classify the algebraic count and Hessian inertia only; higher-order behavior at a zero eigenvalue is not inferred.

For local stability, differentiate the vector field. Its negative Jacobian is L_w. For every x, xᵀL_wx=Σ_e w_e(Bᵀx)_e². With positive w and connected T, this vanishes exactly when x is constant. Hence the common-phase eigenvalue is zero and every mean-zero eigenvalue is positive. This proves transverse linear stability, and the nonlinear conclusion follows directly from a local gradient estimate. On a mean-zero cohesive lift define U(θ)=−bᵀθ−Σ_e K_e cos((Bᵀθ)_e); the rotating-frame dynamics is −∇U. Around a strict cohesive equilibrium choose a sufficiently small convex ball inside a domain |δ_e|≤γ<π/2. Its Hessian is bounded below on 1⊥ by mI with m=cosγ·λ₂(B diag(K)Bᵀ)>0. If x=θ−θ*, then d||x||²/dt≤−2m||x||² in that ball. The vector field points inward on its boundary, so sufficiently near initial states stay there and converge at least as e^(−mt). This is a local argument; no invariance or attraction of the entire cohesive domain has been assumed.

Differentiate arcsin(f_e/K_e) while holding K_e fixed to get ∂δ_e/∂f_e=1/√(K_e²−f_e²)=1/w_e. Because f_e is a linear cut sum of b, this also gives exact frequency sensitivities. Holding the other flows fixed and changing only f_e shifts the phases by a constant on each component of the cut. In the mean-zero gauge, the two constants differ by dδ_e; therefore ||∂θ/∂f_e||₂=√(s(n−s)/n)/w_e. Thus sensitivity diverges as an edge saturates, even though the equilibrium remains locally stable before the boundary.

The rate estimates quantify the same boundary. The inequality L_w≽w_min BBᵀ gives λ₂(L_w)≥w_min λ₂(BBᵀ) by the Rayleigh principle on 1⊥. For the upper bound, use a test vector equal to (n−s)/n on a component of size s and −s/n on the other. Its only nonzero edge difference is one across the removed edge, its squared norm is s(n−s)/n and its energy is w_e. Its Rayleigh quotient is n w_e/[s(n−s)], proving the bound. If one bridge weight tends to zero, the convergence rate therefore tends to zero; the tree is dynamically approaching disconnection in its linearized restoring force.

For observability, let A=−L_w and C=Bᵀ. Then ker C=span{1}, A1=0, and the unobservable linear subspace ⋂_(j≥0)ker(CA^j) is exactly span{1}: the j=0 kernel already gives an upper bound, while common phase survives every power. For sine measurements the local derivative is diag(cosδ*)Bᵀ, whose diagonal factor is invertible under strict cohesion, so the same conclusion holds. Adding an absolute phase measurement e_rᵀ makes the stacked instantaneous observation injective. Separately, replacing ω by ω+c1 changes a solution to θ(t)+ct1 and leaves every relative-phase output unchanged. Relative data can identify b but cannot determine Ω without a time or phase reference.

A stronger blindness example does not rely on common phase. Take a star with center 1 and identical coupling k>0, equal natural frequencies removed by a rotating frame, and at least two leaves. Put θ₁(t)=0, θ₀(t)=a(t), θ₂(t)=−a(t), and all other leaf phases zero, where ȧ=−k sin a. The center receives sin a+sin(−a)=0, and each leaf equation is satisfied. For |a₀|<π, a(t)=2 arctan(tan(a₀/2)e^(−kt)) is an exact solution converging to synchronization. Its center output is identically zero, just as for the equilibrium, so arbitrarily close nonequilibrium states are not identifiable from that output. At linear order, leaf vectors with zero center and zero leaf sum form an (n−2)-dimensional invisible eigenspace with eigenvalue −k. Adding a measurement of one displaced leaf or one of its incident edges detects this particular pair motion, while measuring every edge difference detects all mean-zero states. Thus local convergence and local observability are independent properties even within an exactly solvable stable family.

example.setup: Use vertices 0,1,2,3 with edges oriented 0→1, 1→2, 1→3. Let Ω=2, b=(−1/2,1/6,1/3,0), ω=(3/2,13/6,7/3,2), couplings K=(5/6,13/15,1/2), and cut flows f=(1/2,1/3,0). These are rational input data.
example.calculation:
The incidence equation is Bf=(−f₀,f₀−f₁−f₂,f₁,f₂)=b. The edge sines are s=(3/5,5/13,0), and choose positive cosines c=(4/5,12/13,1). The exact unit phasors are z₀=1, z₁=(4+3i)/5, z₂=(33+56i)/65 and z₃=(4+3i)/5. Their head-tail ratios have precisely those rational real and imaginary parts. Equivalently, choose phases (0,α,α+β,α), where α=arctan(3/4) and β=arctan(5/12), before subtracting the mean. All edge differences are principal and even satisfy |sinδ_e|<4/5, a strict certificate for the cohesive bound γ=arcsin(4/5).

The Hessian weights are w=Kc=(2/3,4/5,1/2). Every principal cofactor of the stable weighted tree Laplacian equals their product 4/15, and its kernel is exactly the common-phase line. The unweighted four-node star has λ₂=1, so the transverse rate obeys 1/2≤λ₂(L_w)≤2/3, the upper bound using the leaf-3 cut. These bounds and the rational Laplacian entries can be checked without evaluating any inverse trigonometric function. Flipping any subset of the three edge cosine signs, while leaving the sine values fixed, constructs all eight phase-locked branches with rational phasors. Their unstable dimensions have counts 1,3,3,1 for indices 0,1,2,3; the stable branch is the sole index-zero case.

Now retain K and the first two flows but replace f₂ by q∈(−1/2,1/2). This changes b to (−1/2,1/6−q,1/3,q). The third weight is w₂(q)=√(1/4−q²), which is always the minimum weight. Consequently w₂(q)≤λ₂(L_w(q))≤(4/3)w₂(q), while dδ₂/dq=1/w₂(q) and the mean-zero phase sensitivity norm is √3/(2w₂(q)). Thus λ₂ times the edge-phase sensitivity stays between 1 and 4/3, while the rate vanishes and sensitivity diverges at either saturation boundary. The rational parametrization q=t/(1+t²), w₂=(1−t²)/(2(1+t²)) for 0≤t<1 supplies exact examples arbitrarily close to the boundary.
example.conclusion: The nonlinear equilibrium, its positive Hessian and its cut-flow certificate are explicit. The parameter family proves a quantitative relation between critical slowing and ill-conditioned phase reconstruction. The separate exact star trajectory proves that a stable network can still be invisible to an inadequate observation panel.

syntheses.limits: The theorem covers symmetric positive couplings on a finite tree and a specified principal cohesive lift. It does not assert global convergence, attraction from arbitrary phases, robustness to noise or delays, or sufficiency of edge bounds on general cycles. At a saturated edge |f_e|=K_e the positive-weight and exponential-stability proof fails; existence at the closed π/2 boundary does not restore its missing rate. The rational verifier certifies finite examples and exact identities, not the general theorem in a proof assistant. The tree-locking criterion is established literature; no novelty claim is made for it.
syntheses.extension: The completed operational consequence is a two-stage certificate: first verify Bf=b and edge feasibility to certify a cohesive equilibrium; then verify the rank of the actual observation map on the mean-zero state space. For a full edge panel the residual blindness is exactly common phase, whereas a center-only symmetric-star panel fails even for exact nonlinear trajectories. If a graph contains cycles, an additional cycle-compatibility problem must be solved before reusing this certificate design.

syntheses.title: The complete one-magnon Gaudin family and its scalar equations
syntheses.status: Classical rank-one structure developed into a proved finite-sector theorem with exact rational and exceptional certificates
syntheses.summary: The two-site calculation extends to an explicit theorem for every number of spin-1/2 sites in the one-magnon sector. Simple critical points of one polynomial give a complete joint eigenbasis. For distinct real sites these critical points necessarily interlace and are simple, so this sector has no missing regular Bethe states apart from the explicitly retained uniform descendant. A three-site rational example is solved on the entire eight-dimensional tensor space, and the complex discriminant-zero locus exhibits a genuine Jordan degeneration.
definitions: Let n≥2, take pairwise distinct complex sites z₁,…,z_n and put p(x)=∏_i(x−z_i). The one-magnon space has basis e_j, meaning that only spin j is down.
Use Ω_ij=(1/2)h_i h_j+e_i f_j+f_i e_j and H_i=Σ_(j≠i)Ω_ij/(z_i−z_j). Define E_i⁰=(1/2)Σ_(j≠i)1/(z_i−z_j) and the uniform vector u=Σ_j e_j.

For w not equal to a site, define a_j(w)=1/(w−z_j), B(w)=Σ_j a_j(w)=p′(w)/p(w), and v(w)=Σ_j a_j(w)e_j. The scalar equation uses u_w(x)=p′(x)/(2p(x))−1/(x−w) and V_w=u_w²−u_w′. The symbol u_w is a scalar connection coefficient and is distinct from the uniform vector u.

result.name: Critical points give a complete spectral decomposition under the stated simple-root condition
result.statement: If p′ has n−1 distinct roots w₁,…,w_(n−1), the vectors u,v(w₁),…,v(w_(n−1)) are a basis of the one-magnon space. Their H_i eigenvalues are E_i⁰ and E_i(w)=E_i⁰+a_i(w), respectively. For distinct real sites, the hypothesis always holds: exactly one critical point lies in each consecutive-site interval. For every critical w, V_w=(3/4)Σ_i(x−z_i)^(−2)+Σ_iE_i(w)/(x−z_i), with no pole at w. Its scalar equation has a rational-over-sqrt(p) fundamental pair of Wronskian one.
result.proof:
The action on a pair of sites is explicit: Ω_ij e_i=−e_i/2+e_j, Ω_ij e_j=e_i−e_j/2, while Ω_ij e_k=e_k/2 if k differs from both. Therefore, for k≠i, the kth component of H_i v(w) is E_i⁰a_k+(a_i−a_k)/(z_i−z_k)=(E_i⁰+a_i)a_k. Its ith component equals E_i⁰a_i−a_iΣ_(j≠i)a_j=(E_i⁰+a_i)a_i−a_iB(w). At a critical point B=0, this is the claimed eigenvector. Directly H_i u=E_i⁰u. For any fixed i, the n displayed eigenvalues are distinct because the map w↦1/(w−z_i) is injective and never zero. They therefore give a basis, proving completeness within this finite sector without assuming it. In particular the H_i are simultaneously diagonal in that basis. For real ordered sites, Rolle’s theorem supplies at least one root of p′ in each of n−1 disjoint gaps. Since deg p′=n−1, these are all its roots, each simple. The vectors are orthogonal: uᵀv(w)=B(w)=0 and v(w)ᵀv(v)=[B(w)−B(v)]/(v−w)=0 for distinct critical roots. Their squared norm is −p″(w)/p(w), which is positive for real sites and nonzero whenever the critical root is simple. Thus P_w=v(w)v(w)ᵀ/[−p″(w)/p(w)] and P₀=uuᵀ/n give explicit spectral projectors.

For the scalar equation, a physical site z_i has u_w=1/[2(x−z_i)]+E_i(w)+O(x−z_i), so V_w has double coefficient 3/4 and simple residue E_i(w). At x=w, write u_w=−1/(x−w)+B(w)/2+O(x−w); the double pole cancels and the simple residue is −B(w), hence zero at a Bethe root. Since V_w decays at infinity, its partial fractions are exactly the asserted expression. One solution is y₁=(x−w)/sqrt(p(x)). Reduction of order gives y₂=y₁∫p(x)/(x−w)² dx. Taylor expansion at w has no linear term because p′(w)=0, so an explicit numerator is q₂(x)=−p(w)+Σ_(m=2)^n p^(m)(w)(x−w)^m/[m!(m−1)]. Then y₂=q₂/sqrt(p), and y₁y₂′−y₁′y₂=1. Both solutions are regular at the apparent point w. Their only multivalued factor is a common square root, so the resulting monodromy is scalar and projectively trivial. This is a concrete scalar-oper statement with all normalizations fixed.

example.setup: Take three sites z=(0,1,8/3), and separately study z=(0,1,t) as a complex parameter family.
example.calculation:
For z=(0,1,8/3), p′ has roots 2 and4/9. Their highest one-magnon coefficient vectors are (1/2,1,−3/2) and (9/4,−9/5,−9/20), giving Hamiltonian triples (−3/16,6/5,−81/80) and (25/16,−8/5,3/80). Each generates a two-dimensional spin doublet under total lowering. The vacuum generates a quartet with triple (−11/16,1/5,39/80). The verifier constructs all eight rational eigenvectors and all three full 8×8 Hamiltonians, verifies joint eigenvector relations and rank eight, and checks both scalar differential equations through identically zero residual polynomials and Wronskians. As another independent exact example, four sites (−7,−1,1,7) have critical roots (−5,0,5), so their complete four-dimensional one-magnon diagonalization and three scalar solution pairs remain rational.

For z=(0,1,t), p′=3x²−2(1+t)x+t and its root discriminant is 4(t²−t+1). The exceptional sites are t=(1±i√3)/2. They are distinct from 0 and1, but the two Bethe roots coalesce at w=(1+t)/3. Here B(w)=B′(w)=0. Differentiating the exact off-shell relation gives (H_i−E_i(w))v′(w)=−a_i(w)²v(w). The right side is nonzero, and v′ is independent of v because distinct sites prevent all a_j from being equal. Together with u these vectors span the three-dimensional sector, so each H_i has a size-two Jordan block there. The checker works exactly in Q(t) with t²−t+1=0 rather than relying on near-coincident numerical eigenvalues.
example.conclusion: The finite real-site completeness theorem is closed under its stated assumptions. The three-site complex exceptional locus is also explicit, and its loss of diagonalizability is certified by generalized eigenvectors. The scalar-oper formula survives there, but it cannot by itself distinguish the generalized direction in a nonreduced spectral problem.

syntheses.limits: The general theorem covers one-magnon states and the uniform descendant, not every magnetization sector for arbitrary n. The full eight-dimensional completeness statement applies only to the explicitly checked three-site example. General higher-rank Gaudin opers, arbitrary representations and a global Langlands correspondence require additional theory. Projectively trivial scalar monodromy here follows from the explicit fundamental pair, not from a broad assertion that all ODEs associated with a spin system have trivial monodromy.
syntheses.extension: S014 completes the distinct-complex-site one-magnon Jordan classification, including arbitrary critical multiplicities and a closed characteristic formula. For multi-magnon sectors the Bethe equations include root-root interactions. A disciplined next step is to compute a finite highest-weight multiplicity space independently, then compare regular, singular and generalized Bethe vectors with its exact joint spectrum. The exceptional-point calculation shows why a scheme-level spectrum may contain information that a set of distinct eigenvalues loses.

syntheses.title: Minimum induced subgraph order and the sharp heat observation margin
syntheses.status: Exact finite classification and analytic margin proved
syntheses.summary: The rook–Shrikhande collision can be pushed beyond merely producing two graphs with the same spectrum. For this pair, every permutation-invariant induced-subgraph count through order three agrees, all eleven four-vertex pattern counts are classified, and a single labeled off-diagonal heat observation has a sharp optimal time and a sharp worst-case error threshold. These are different observation classes and must not be conflated.
definitions: For a finite simple graph G and an unlabeled k-vertex graph H, N_H(G) is the number of k-element subsets of V(G) whose induced graph is isomorphic to H. Dividing by C(|V(G)|,k) gives the distribution obtained by uniform vertex-subset sampling.
The feature panel through order d is the vector of all N_H(G) for all unlabeled H with at most d vertices. This vector is invariant under relabeling G.
The two candidate graphs R and S are the sixteen-vertex rook and Shrikhande graphs from M020. Their vertices are assigned the known coordinate labels in Z₄².
For the separate labeled observation problem, observe y=(exp(−tL))_{uv}+η at t>0, with known u=(0,0), v=(0,2) and adversarial error |η|≤ε.

result.name: A feature-class lower bound and an optimal labeled experiment
result.statement: The feature panels through order three coincide for R and S; the order-four panels differ, so four is the minimum distinguishing order within this feature class. Their K₄ counts are eight and zero. For the known labels u,v, the heat-entry difference is d(t)=(e^(−4t)−e^(−8t))/4. It has unique maximum 1/16 at t*=log(2)/4. At that time the candidate observations are 5/64 and 1/64. Uniform identification under the stated bounded-error model is possible exactly when ε<1/32.
result.proof:
For any strongly regular graph with parameters (v,k,λ,μ), the number of edges is vk/2 and the triangle count is vkλ/6. Each vertex contributes C(k,2) neighbor pairs; subtracting its kλ/2 neighbor-neighbor edges counts induced three-vertex paths centered there, so their total is v[C(k,2)−kλ/2]. For an edge, the vertices adjacent to neither endpoint number v−2k+λ, giving (vk/2)(v−2k+λ) induced single-edge triples. Subtract these three classes from C(v,3) to obtain the independent triples. With (16,6,2,2), these counts are respectively triangles32, paths144, single-edge triples288 and independent triples96. The vertex, edge, nonedge and empty-set counts also agree. Therefore every function of the specified feature panel of order at most three agrees; no decision rule using only that panel can separate the pair. A four-clique occurs on each row and each column of the rook graph, giving eight. The exhaustive canonical certificate finds none in Shrikhande, proving that order four suffices. It classifies all 1,820 four-subsets in each graph rather than checking only one witness.

For the heat formula, both adjacency matrices satisfy A²=4I+2J. On the constant vector the heat operator acts by one; on the adjacency eigenvalues +2 and −2 it acts by a=e^(−4t) and b=e^(−8t). Solving for its coefficients in span{I,A,J} gives K_t=((a+b)/2)I+((a−b)/4)A+((1−2a+b)/16)J. The aligned pair is an edge of R and a nonedge of S, so their difference is (a−b)/4. Put x=e^(−4t)∈(0,1): d=x(1−x)/4=1/16−(x−1/2)²/4. This proves the unique maximum and its time without numerical optimization. At x=1/2, the common nonedge value is 1/64 and adding the edge coefficient gives 5/64.

Under either hypothesis the possible noisy values form a closed interval of radius ε around its candidate value. These intervals are disjoint exactly when 2ε<1/16. The midpoint threshold 3/64 then separates them for every permitted error. At ε=1/32 both hypotheses can produce the midpoint: subtract 1/32 from 5/64 or add 1/32 to 1/64. No deterministic or randomized classifier can guarantee correct identification from that indistinguishable observation. Larger error budgets also contain this ambiguity.

example.setup: Canonicalize a labeled four-vertex graph by enumerating all twenty-four vertex permutations and taking the smallest six-edge bit mask. First enumerate all sixty-four labeled four-vertex graphs to obtain the complete set of eleven canonical classes; then classify every four-subset of R and S.
example.calculation: The counts in canonical-mask order are empty24/16, one-edge-plus-two-isolates288/336, path-plus-isolate576/480, star0/32, triangle-plus-isolate96/128, two-disjoint-edges216/192, four-path288/384, triangle-with-pendant288/192, four-cycle36/12, diamond0/48 and four-clique8/0, where each pair is rook/Shrikhande. Each column sums to 1,820. These exact distributions are stored in supplement_checks.json. At the optimal heat time the shared diagonal is 25/64, the edge value5/64 and nonedge value1/64; 25/64+6(5/64)+9(1/64)=1 verifies the row-sum normalization.
example.conclusion: The pair is completely indistinguishable by induced pattern counts of orders zero through three, yet every four-vertex class count differs. A labeled heat entry is a different feature and can separate the same aligned candidates with one scalar observation.

syntheses.limits: The minimum-order statement is restricted to the declared induced-subgraph count panels; it is not a universal lower bound on all graph invariants, sensors, computational algorithms or sample counts. The heat threshold assumes exact time control, fixed known vertex correspondence, the two stated candidate graphs and the bounded-error model. It proves neither recovery of an unknown unlabeled graph nor uniform stability of taking a matrix logarithm. An unknown vertex permutation can change which pair is an edge and must be included as a nuisance parameter in a different problem. The continuous optimum t*=log(2)/4 is exact; numerical time selection incurs a separate margin loss.
syntheses.extension: The exact loss from a known mistiming t=t*+h is 1/16−d(t)=(e^(−4h)−1)²/16. If the actual time is observed but the design must tolerate |h|≤δ<t*, the worst same-time gap is [1−(e^(4δ)−1)²]/16, and a threshold adjusted to the observed time works for errors less than half that gap. If the actual time is unobserved, that bound alone is insufficient: each hypothesis ranges over different possible times. Put l=e^(−4δ)/2 and u=e^(4δ)/2. Over that interval, the least rook entry is (1+2u−3u²)/16, while the greatest Shrikhande entry is (1−l)²/16. The uniformly separating interval gap is therefore Δ=[2(u+l)−3u²−l²]/16, when positive, and the admissible bounded error is ε<Δ/2. These extrema follow because the Shrikhande entry decreases in x and the rook entry is concave; the difference of its endpoint values has sign (u−l)[2−3(u+l)]<0. For δ=log(3/2)/4, the exact candidate-set endpoints are 13/256 and 1/36, giving Δ=53/2304 and ε<53/4608. Thus calibrated deviation and an unobserved timing nuisance are genuinely different robustness problems. No version of these bounds establishes uniform unlabeled graph recovery.

syntheses.title: Singular quadratic duality requires an observation quotient
syntheses.status: Classical convex duality proved with a complete finite-dimensional classification and exact certificates
syntheses.summary: A pseudoinverse cannot simply replace an inverse inside every constrained-energy formula. Zero-energy input directions can generate nonzero observed outputs, and these free outputs must be quotiented out before applying the usual minimum-energy expression. The same geometry explains the finite domain of the Fenchel conjugate, the divergent part of ridge regularization, and changes in rank or active constraints. This supplies an algebraic complement to the positive-definite projection calculation in S006; it is a classical result developed here, not a claim of a new duality theorem.
definitions: Work in finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces. Let Q=Qᵀ≥0 be n×n, f(x)=xᵀQx/2, N=kerQ and R=N⊥=rangeQ. The Moore–Penrose inverse Q⁺ inverts Q on R and is zero on N.
For B:Rⁿ→Rᵐ and output z∈Rᵐ, define the output space W=BN generated at zero energy. Let P be the Euclidean orthogonal projection onto W⊥ and put H=PBQ⁺BᵀP. This H is symmetric positive semidefinite.

The equality-constrained value is v(z)=inf{f(x):Bx=z}, with value +∞ if infeasible. Inequalities are not part of this general formula; the separately stated parameter example includes x≥0 and has its own KKT certificates.
The Fenchel conjugate is f*(y)=sup_x(yᵀx−f(x)). For ε>0, the ridge energy is f_ε(x)=xᵀ(Q+εI)x/2. Its conjugate is finite everywhere.

result.name: Conjugate domain, ridge limit and complete equality-constrained value
result.statement: The conjugate is f*(y)=yᵀQ⁺y/2 for y∈R, and +∞ otherwise. Writing y=y_R+y_N, the ridge conjugate is f_ε*(y)=y_Rᵀ(Q|_R+εI_R)⁻¹y_R/2+||y_N||²/(2ε). Thus it tends to f*(y), with an explicit 1/ε divergence off R. The equation Bx=z is feasible exactly when Pz∈rangeH, equivalently z∈rangeB. When feasible, v(z)=(Pz)ᵀH⁺(Pz)/2. Its unique minimum-energy R-component is r*=Q⁺BᵀP H⁺Pz. Choose n*∈N with Bn*=z−Br*. All minimizers are r*+n*+(N∩kerB). A dual optimizer is λ*=H⁺Pz; the dual admissibility condition is Bᵀλ∈R, equivalently λ∈W⊥. If feasibility fails, the dual is unbounded above along an explicitly separating direction.
result.proof:
First split x=r+n orthogonally with r∈R and n∈N. Since Qn=0, yᵀx−f(x)=y_Rᵀr−rᵀQr/2+y_Nᵀn. If y_N≠0, choosing n=t y_N and sending t→+∞ proves that the supremum is infinite. If y_N=0, Q is positive definite on R, and completing the square there gives the unique maximizing r=Q⁺y and value yᵀQ⁺y/2; any null component of x is allowed. Diagonalizing Q separately on R and N yields the ridge formula. If Q has smallest positive eigenvalue a, then on R the finite ridge error obeys 0≤f*(y_R)−f_ε*(y_R)≤ε||y_R||²/(2a²). No such finite uniform limit exists for a fixed nonzero y_N because its contribution is exactly ||y_N||²/(2ε).

Next write Bx=Br+Bn. A null component can supply precisely W, so the constraint is equivalent to PBr=Pz. On R set u=(Q|_R)^(1/2)r and C=PB(Q|_R)^(−1/2), interpreted as a map from R to W⊥. The energy is ||u||²/2 and the quotient constraint is Cu=Pz. Since H=CCᵀ, rangeH=rangeC: their orthogonal complements both equal ker Cᵀ, because aᵀHa=||Cᵀa||². Thus feasibility is exactly the stated range test. For a feasible right side, the least-norm solution is u*=CᵀH⁺Pz. Indeed Cu*=HH⁺Pz=Pz, and u* lies in range Cᵀ, orthogonal to every feasible increment in kerC. Pythagoras proves uniqueness and the value ||u*||²/2=(Pz)ᵀH⁺Pz/2. Returning to r gives the displayed formula. The residual z−Br* lies in kerP=W, so a suitable n* exists. Strict convexity on R fixes r*, while all permissible null components differ by N∩kerB.

For the dual, use L(x,λ)=f(x)+λᵀ(z−Bx). Taking the infimum over x gives d(λ)=λᵀz−f*(Bᵀλ). The finite-domain condition says λ annihilates BN: nᵀBᵀλ=0 for every n∈N. Therefore λ=Pλ and d(λ)=λᵀPz−λᵀHλ/2. At λ*=H⁺Pz, stationarity and feasibility give Qx*=Bᵀλ*, Bx*=z, and primal and dual values agree. This proves strong duality directly without relying on an unstated constraint qualification. If Pz is outside rangeH, let a be its nonzero projection onto kerH∩W⊥. Then Bᵀa lies in R and aᵀHa=0 forces Bᵀa=0. The dual ray λ=ta has d(ta)=t||a||²→+∞, while aᵀz≠0 proves Bx=z impossible. These are both an infeasibility certificate and a dual-geometry explanation.

The simpler expression zᵀ(BQ⁺Bᵀ)⁺z/2 is valid without the quotient when BN={0}, together with the feasibility condition z∈range(BQ⁺Bᵀ). Dropping either condition can give a wrong finite value. The case Q=0 is covered: every feasible output is free, H=0 and the value is zero, while infeasible outputs have value +∞.

example.setup: First use Q=diag(2,0,3), B=[[1,1,0],[0,1,1]] and z=(1,0). Then examine the parameter family Q_t=diag(1,t,0), b_a=(1,1,a), equality b_a x=1, and, as a distinct program, the extra constraint x≥0, for t≥0 and a∈R.
example.calculation:
In the two-output example N=span(e₂), W=span((1,1)) and P=[[1,−1],[−1,1]]/2. Direct exact multiplication gives H=(5/24)[[1,−1],[−1,1]] and H⁺=(6/5)[[1,−1],[−1,1]]. Therefore λ*=(6/5,−6/5), r*=(3/5,0,−2/5), n*=(0,2/5,0), and x*=(3/5,2/5,−2/5). Its energy and dual value are both 3/5. The raw matrix BQ⁺Bᵀ=diag(1/2,1/3) would instead give the incorrect naive value one. An independent elimination sets x=(1−s,s,−s), giving energy 1−2s+(5/2)s², whose unique minimizer is s=2/5. This verifies both the quotient formula and the counterexample without using pseudoinverse numerical software.

For the parameter family with equality only, Q_t has rank two for t>0 and rank one at t=0. If t>0 and a≠0, x=(0,0,1/a) is feasible and has zero energy. If t>0 and a=0, the minimum is t/[2(1+t)], attained at x₁=t/(1+t), x₂=1/(1+t), with arbitrary x₃. At t=0 the free second coordinate makes the minimum zero for every a. The raw pseudoinverse expression gives t/[2(1+t)] for every a when t>0 and gives 1/2 at t=0. Thus it is wrong on entire parameter strata, not merely at an isolated numerical accident.

Now impose x≥0. For t>0,a>0, the unique minimizer is (0,0,1/a), with energy zero. For t>0,a=0, all minimizers are (t/(1+t),1/(1+t),s), s≥0, with value t/[2(1+t)]. For t>0,a<0, the unique minimizer is (t/(1+t),1/(1+t),0), with the same positive value. To certify the latter two branches choose λ=t/(1+t), ν=(0,0,−aλ) and stationarity Q_t x−λb_a−ν=0. For a≤0, ν≥0, and complementary slackness holds; at a=0 its third multiplier vanishes. For a>0 choose λ=0,ν=0 at the zero-energy minimizer. At t=0 every feasible vector with x₁=0 is optimal: if a>0 this is the segment x₃∈[0,1/a], x₂=1−ax₃; if a≤0 it is the ray x₃≥0, x₂=1−ax₃. These zero-energy branches also have λ=ν=0 certificates. For example t=2,a=−1 has constrained optimum (2/3,1/3,0), value 1/3 and ν₃=2/3, whereas its equality-only optimum (0,0,−1) has value zero.

For every listed nonnegative candidate, convexity makes these KKT certificates globally sufficient: for any other feasible x=x*+h, the objective difference equals hᵀQ_th/2+νᵀx≥0. This is a proof for all real parameters in the declared strata; the verifier replays representative rational points and checks feasibility, stationarity, nonnegative multipliers, complementarity and primal–dual agreement exactly. As a→0 from above at fixed t>0, the zero-energy minimizer escapes to infinity while the value jumps upward at a=0. The discontinuity comes from loss of uniform control of null directions, not from a failure of the theorem.
example.conclusion: The dual must discard observed outputs that can be supplied without energy, by restricting multipliers to their annihilator. Inequalities can prevent use of those directions, which is why a linear nullspace quotient alone is not a formula for an inequality-constrained problem. Rank, output compatibility and active constraints form separate strata. This makes the relation to M062 and M093 precise and complements S006 without conflating zero energy, zero variance and missing statistical information.

syntheses.limits: Everything here is finite-dimensional with a symmetric positive-semidefinite quadratic form and exact equality constraints. In an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space the range need not be closed and minimizers or bounded pseudoinverses may fail to exist. An indefinite Q can make the primal unbounded below. The nonnegative parameter family is solved separately by KKT; the quotient formula does not automatically incorporate general inequalities. A ridge limit is a declared regularization, not a justification for deleting divergent terms or for replacing inverses by pseudoinverses without range tests.
syntheses.extension: For rational parameter-dependent Q and B, produce exact rank strata, bases for kerQ and BkerQ, compatibility equations for Pz and KKT active-set certificates. Preserve both the domain conditions and the optimizer set at boundary parameters. In a statistical application specify whether Q describes energy, precision or covariance before transferring these algebraic formulas into a measurement claim.

syntheses.title: An exact exceptional point and its two-sheeted spectral cover
syntheses.status: Finite parameter-family classification and exact Jordan/projector certificates; no novelty claim
syntheses.summary: The three-site sl₂ Gaudin family has an explicit exceptional locus where two highest-weight eigenlines coalesce. At that locus a genuine Jordan block replaces the two eigenvectors. Nearby spectral projectors diverge although their sum stays constant. Analytic continuation of the eigenvalue labels exchanges the two lines. This is spectral-cover monodromy in a parameter, not monodromy of a KZ connection or of the scalar differential equation in its spatial variable.
definitions: Use the one-magnon sector and normalization of S010, with sites z=(0,1,t), t≠0,1. Put p_t(x)=x(x−1)(x−t), D(t)=t²−t+1 and w±=(1+t±sqrt(D))/3.
For D≠0, let v± have components 1/(w±−z_j), and E_i±=E_i⁰+1/(w±−z_i). The uniform vector is u=(1,1,1)ᵀ and the highest-weight projection is Q=I−uuᵀ/3.

Transpose is the complex bilinear transpose, not the Hermitian adjoint. For complex t the resulting spectral projectors need not be orthogonal for the standard Hermitian norm. Their divergence is compatible with Q remaining bounded.

result.name: Jordan degeneration, projector cancellation and spectral-label exchange
result.statement: The only critical-root collisions in this family occur at t₀=(1±i√3)/2, the simple zeros of D. At t=t₀, w₀=(1+t₀)/3 and v₀=v(w₀) satisfy (H_i−E_i)v₀=0 and (H_i−E_i)v′₀=−a_i²v₀, where a_i=1/(w₀−z_i). Thus each H_i has a size-two Jordan block on im Q. For D≠0, P±=∓p_t(w±)v±v±ᵀ/(2sqrt(D)), and P++P−=Q exactly. As t approaches t₀ on either local sheet, sqrt(D)P+→−p_(t₀)(w₀)v₀v₀ᵀ/2 and sqrt(D)P− has the opposite limit. A loop encircling just one zero of D exchanges P+ and P−.
result.proof:
Differentiating p_t gives p′=3x²−2(1+t)x+t, so the critical roots have the displayed quadratic formula. Its discriminant vanishes precisely at the two stated sites, and D′(t₀)=2t₀−1≠0. At the collision B=p′/p and B′ both vanish at w₀, while p(w₀)≠0 because the physical sites are still distinct. The off-shell identity from S010 is H_i v(w)=E_i(w)v(w)−a_i(w)B(w)e_i. Differentiating in w at fixed t₀ eliminates both residual terms and gives the generalized-eigenvector relation, with E_i′=−a_i²≠0. If v′ were proportional to v, all a_j would have to be equal, contrary to distinct sites. Both vectors have coordinate sum zero; with u they span the full sector. Therefore the block is genuinely Jordan, not a repeated diagonal eigenvalue.

At a simple critical root the bilinear square is v(w)ᵀv(w)=−p″(w)/p(w). Since p″(w±)=±2sqrt(D), the projector formula follows. The eigenvectors u,v+,v− form a bilinear-orthogonal basis when D≠0, so their projectors sum to I and P++P−=Q. The numerator of P+ tends to a nonzero rank-one matrix, giving divergence proportional to |D|^(−1/2) in any fixed finite-dimensional matrix norm. With ε=sqrt(D), one has t−t₀=O(ε²), w±=w₀±ε/3+O(ε²), and p_t(w±)=p_(t₀)(w₀)+O(ε²). Thus P±=∓p₀v₀v₀ᵀ/(2ε)−p₀(v′₀v₀ᵀ+v₀v′₀ᵀ)/6+O(ε). The divergent terms cancel. In fact Q=−p₀(v′₀v₀ᵀ+v₀v′₀ᵀ)/3 at the exceptional point. The finite surviving nilpotent is N_i=(H_i−E_i)Q=(p₀a_i²/3)v₀v₀ᵀ. It is nonzero and N_i²=0 because v₀ᵀv₀=0.

Finally D=(t−t₀)(t−t₁). A sufficiently small loop around t₀ winds D once around zero because t₁ lies outside. Analytic continuation of sqrt(D) therefore changes sign, exchanging the two roots, eigenvalues and projectors. This proof concerns the two-sheeted algebraic spectral cover; it introduces no connection or parallel-transport operator.

example.setup: Perform the exceptional calculation exactly in K=Q(τ), τ²−τ+1=0, taking t₀=τ and w₀=(1+τ)/3.
example.calculation: The supplemental verifier constructs all three 3×3 Hamiltonians over K. It checks their commutators, the eigenvector and generalized-eigenvector identities, rank(u,v₀,v′₀)=3, the constant-projector formula and N_i=(p₀a_i²/3)v₀v₀ᵀ with N_i≠0 and N_i²=0. These are exact algebraic calculations, independent of numerical eigenvalue separation. Additional complex-number evaluations approach the exceptional point along D=ε² and check the leading projector coefficient and cancellation. A separately tracked square root around a small parameter loop exchanges the two labels, agreeing with the analytic winding argument.
example.conclusion: This closes the finite three-site exceptional-point question: location, Jordan structure, projector blowup, cancellation and label exchange are explicit. The exact field certificate carries the algebraic result; numerical paths illustrate its limiting and continuation behavior.

syntheses.limits: For real distinct sites, D=(t−1/2)²+3/4 is positive and cannot reach this exceptional locus; the real-site orthogonal projectors therefore do not develop this singularity. The result does not classify every higher-site exceptional locus. Spectral-cover label exchange, spatial scalar-ODE monodromy and KZ connection monodromy are three different constructions and must not be identified.
syntheses.extension: S014 completes the distinct-site one-magnon answer: each multiplicity-m root of p′ gives exactly one size-m Jordan block, and the commuting spectral algebra retains its nilpotent direction. Further work should address multi-magnon sectors or collisions of the physical sites, where the present hypotheses and one-coordinate construction do not apply unchanged.

syntheses.title: Complete complex one-magnon Jordan classification
syntheses.status: Proved finite-sector classification with exact Gaussian-rational examples; classical framework, no global novelty claim
syntheses.summary: The simple-critical-point qualification in S010 can be removed. For arbitrary distinct complex spin-1/2 sites, multiplicities of the roots of p′ determine all Jordan block sizes in the one-magnon sector. One explicit local coordinate turns the Bethe vector’s derivatives into a Jordan chain of the correct length. The chains exhaust the sector, and every Hamiltonian generates the same finite commuting algebra after polynomial interpolation.
definitions: Retain p(x)=∏_(j=1)^n(x−z_j), H_i and E_i⁰ from S010, with all physical sites distinct. A critical root w_r has multiplicity m_r as a root of p′. Since p has simple roots, p(w_r)≠0; Σ_r m_r=n−1.
Fix any Hamiltonian index i. At w_r write a=1/(w_r−z_i), use local coordinate q=1/(w−z_i)−a, and define w(q)=z_i+1/(a+q). Expand v(w(q))=Σ_(k≥0)V_(r,k)q^k near q=0.

A length-m Jordan chain for H−E is a list V₀,…,V_(m−1) with (H−E)V₀=0 and (H−E)V_k=V_(k−1) for k≥1. No factorial is missing: V_k is the Taylor coefficient, equivalently the kth derivative divided by k!.

result.name: Critical multiplicity equals Jordan length for every H_i
result.statement: On the n-dimensional one-magnon space, each H_i has one uniform-descendant block of size one and eigenvalue E_i⁰, together with exactly one block of size m_r and eigenvalue E_i(r)=E_i⁰+1/(w_r−z_i) for each distinct critical root w_r. Consequently H_i is diagonalizable exactly when p′ is squarefree, and its minimal polynomial equals its characteristic polynomial of degree n. With A_i=H_i−E_i⁰I, one has A_j=A_i[I+(z_i−z_j)A_i]⁻¹. The characteristic polynomial is χ_Hi(λ)=u^n p′(z_i+1/u)/p′(z_i), u=λ−E_i⁰, interpreted by polynomial expansion. The unital algebra generated by the H_j is C[H_i], isomorphic to C×∏_r C[q]/(q^(m_r)).
result.proof:
The exact off-shell identity is H_i v(w)=(E_i⁰+a_i(w))v(w)−a_i(w)B(w)e_i, with B=p′/p. At a multiplicity-m critical root, B(w) vanishes to order m. The local coordinate q is valid because a_i′(w_r)=−a²≠0, and its inverse is the displayed rational function. Moreover E_i(w(q))=E_i(r)+q exactly. Thus (H_i−E_i(r))v(w(q))=q v(w(q))+O(q^m). Equating Taylor coefficients through q^(m−1) gives the claimed chain. It is independent: if a linear relation has highest nonzero coefficient at V_k, applying (H_i−E_i(r))^k leaves that coefficient times V₀, a contradiction because V₀≠0. Distinct critical roots have distinct E_i(r), since w↦1/(w−z_i) is injective; none equals E_i⁰. Their generalized eigenspaces and the uniform vector are therefore independent. Their dimensions total 1+Σm_r=n, so they form a complete basis and no larger or additional block can exist.

For any other j, put d=z_i−z_j and A=1+da. This A is nonzero because w_r is not a physical site. In the same coordinate, a_j(w(q))=(a+q)/(A+dq)=a_j(w_r)+Σ_(ℓ≥1)c_jℓ q^ℓ, where c_jℓ=(−d)^(ℓ−1)/A^(ℓ+1). The off-shell remainder still has order m. Hence H_j on the chain is E_j(r)I+Σ_(ℓ=1)^(m−1)c_jℓ N^ℓ, with NV_k=V_(k−1). Its linear coefficient is c_j1=A^(−2)≠0, so its nilpotent part is N times an invertible polynomial in N and has the same Jordan length and generalized-eigenspace flags. Equivalently these jets give A_j=A_i(I+dA_i)⁻¹ on each block and on the uniform vector. The denominator is invertible: its critical eigenvalues are (w_r−z_j)/(w_r−z_i), all nonzero, and its uniform eigenvalue is one. An inverse of this finite matrix is polynomial in A_i, giving C[H_i] as the entire generated algebra. Finally χ=u∏_r(u−1/(w_r−z_i))^(m_r); substituting the factorization p′(x)=n∏_r(x−w_r)^(m_r) gives the displayed polynomial formula. The degree-n minimal polynomial and the Chinese remainder theorem yield the algebra decomposition. This proves the entire finite-sector classification, including its nonsemisimple cases.

example.setup: Take four physical sites (1,−1,i,−i), so p=x⁴−1 and p′=4x³. Fix i to be the site z_i=1.
example.calculation:
There is one critical root w=0 of multiplicity three. Its chain coefficients are V₀=(−1,1,i,−i), V₁=(1,1,−1,−1), V₂=(0,2,−1−i,−1+i). The uniform vector and these three vectors have rank four. The eigenvalues are E_j⁰=3/(4z_j) and E_j=−1/(4z_j). In particular H_i has characteristic and minimal polynomial (λ−3/4)(λ+1/4)³. On Q=I−uuᵀ/4, N=(H_i+I/4)Q obeys N³=0 and N²≠0. All equations are checked exactly in Q(i).

A mixed-multiplicity example uses eight distinct sites ±1,±i,±2,±2i, giving p=(x⁴−1)(x⁴−16)=x⁸−17x⁴+16 and p′=4x³(2x⁴−17). The critical multiplicities are three at zero and one at each of four nonzero roots. Thus each H_i has block sizes 3,1,1,1,1,1, including the uniform block. At base site1, E_i⁰=37/60 and E_i(0)=−23/60. If q=λ−37/60, its characteristic polynomial is (λ−37/60)(λ+23/60)³[17q⁴−2(q+1)⁴]/15. The verifier independently calculates the full 8×8 characteristic polynomial by trace/Newton identities over Q(i), checks this factorization and the length-three chain. The four remaining factors have distinct roots because the map w↦1/(w−1) is injective on the four simple roots of 2w⁴−17.
example.conclusion: The multiplicity-three and mixed examples verify higher Jordan lengths and coexistence of simple and nonsimple blocks. The arbitrary-n result is supplied by the proof, not extrapolated from those matrices.

syntheses.limits: This classification concerns the one-magnon sector for distinct physical sites and the stated spin-1/2 quadratic Gaudin Hamiltonians. It does not settle multi-magnon completeness, higher representations, collisions of physical sites, or a global Langlands correspondence. The direct-product algebra is a finite spectral algebra, not a claim that a general moduli space has been constructed.
syntheses.extension: In multi-magnon sectors, root-root interactions and admissibility conditions prevent this one-coordinate argument from being transferred unchanged. An appropriate next problem is to seek an equally explicit off-shell jet construction on a fixed small multiplicity space and compare it against an independently computed joint Jordan form.
